title: API Versioning
subtitle: Evolving APIs safely without breaking existing mobile and third-party clients via URI paths, headers, and date-based pinned versions.
keyTakeaways: Once an API is consumed by external third parties or deployed mobile apps (where users don't update for months), breaking changes require explicit versioning.
Additive changes (adding new optional request fields or new response properties) are backward-compatible; renaming, removing, or changing field types is a breaking change.

URI Path Versioning (`/v1/orders`) is the most pragmatic and debuggable industry standard, while Stripe-style Date Header Pinning (`Stripe-Version: 2026-03-01`) excels for complex developer platforms.

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: Every successful API eventually needs to change a data structure, for example, splitting a single `name: string` field into `first_name` and `last_name`, or changing a synchronous response into an asynchronous job. Because you cannot force every customer or iOS user on a 2-year-old app version to deploy simultaneously, you must support multiple contract versions concurrently during a deprecation window.
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: Once an API is consumed by external third parties or deployed mobile apps (where users don't update for months), breaking changes require explicit versioning.

**Problem Space & Invariants**: Additive changes (adding new optional request fields or new response properties) are backward-compatible; renaming, removing, or changing field types is a breaking change.
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: Distributed architectures apply specific implementation patterns and topologies for API Versioning:
bullets: **URI Path Versioning (/v1/resources, /v2/resources)**: Provides 100% explicit in curl, logs, documentation, and api gateway routing rules; impossible for a developer to miss which version they are calling. Best suited for 90% of public REST APIs, microservice endpoints, and mobile backend APIs.

**Header-Based Date Versioning (X-API-Version: 2026-03-01)**: Provides allows fine-grained, incremental breaking changes via composable request/response migration gates without changing urls. Best suited for Developer-first API platforms (Stripe, Twilio, GitHub) with hundreds of evolving endpoints and per-account version pinning.
1. URI Path Versioning (`/v1/users`, `/v2/users`): Explicit, visible in browser bars and server logs, trivial to route in any L7 Load Balancer or CDN.
2. Header / Media-Type Versioning (`Accept: application/vnd.company.v2+json` or `X-API-Version: 2026-03-01`): Keeps resource URLs pure and unchanging across versions.

Expand-and-Contract: First add the new field (`full_name`) alongside the old field (`name`), dual-populate both for 6 months while monitoring usage metrics, then remove the old field only when traffic hits 0%.
Sunset Headers: Return `Deprecation: true` and `Sunset: Wed, 11 Nov 2026 23:59:59 GMT` so client SDKs log automated warnings.

sections.heading: 3. Production Strengths: Where & How to Apply
sections.body: Production deployments apply API Versioning across targeted operational scenarios:
bullets: **Where to Use: High-Impact Scenarios**: Optimal for 90% of public REST APIs, microservice endpoints, and mobile backend APIs, suited for environments requiring 100% explicit in curl, logs, documentation, and API gateway routing rules; impossible for a developer to miss which version they are calling.

**Where to Use: High-Throughput Scenarios**: Recommended for Developer-first API platforms (Stripe, Twilio, GitHub) with hundreds of evolving endpoints and per-account version pinning, where Allows fine-grained, incremental breaking changes via composable request/response migration gates without changing URLs.

**How to Use: Engineering Implementation**: Creating `/v2` by copy-pasting your entire controller directory leads to maintenance bankruptcy. Always establish explicit thresholds, measurement baselines, and automated monitoring.
**Architectural Leverage**: Provides predictable resource boundaries, bounds blast radius, and optimizes cost per transaction.

sections.heading: 4. Failure Modes & Trade-Offs: When to Avoid
sections.body: Improper implementation of API Versioning introduces operational bottlenecks and failure modes:
bullets: **Where to Avoid: Trade-Off Bottlenecks**: Avoid when constraints cannot tolerate: coarse-grained (bumping `/v2` usually implies versioning the whole api surface); changes resource uris when upgrading.

**Where to Avoid: Complexity Ceiling**: Avoid when operational requirements do not justify: requires building a version-transformation pipeline in the gateway; harder to test casually in a browser address bar.
**Catastrophic Failure Modes**: Uncalibrated parameters can trigger queue exhaustion, thread starvation, cascading retry storms, and tail latency amplification.
**Operational Overhead**: Requires continuous observability (p95/p99 latency tracking, saturation alerts, and distributed tracing across hop boundaries).

sections.heading: 5. Staff+ Engineering Verdict & Interview Playbook
sections.body: Technical guidelines and evaluation criteria for API Versioning:
bullets: **Staff+ Golden Rule**: URI Path Versioning (`/v1/orders`) is the most pragmatic and debuggable industry standard, while Stripe-style Date Header Pinning (`Stripe-Version: 2026-03-01`) excels for complex developer platforms.

**Staff+ Interview Playbook**: In a system design interview, always prefix your endpoints with `/v1/.` (e.g., `POST /v1/bookings`) automatically without waiting to be asked. It takes 3 characters and shows production discipline.
